title: Service-preserving soft-shedding with QoS lanes and token-aware admission hints
creator: Aditi Rao
description:
Problem: During regional capacity spikes and cross-region failover we observe cascading latency and token-cost blowups when large requests queue on hot shards. Existing shedding strategies are either too coarse (hard reject) or too lossy (full model fallback) and cause elevated customer P99 violations or cost surprises.

Goal: Implement a service-preserving soft-shedding mechanism that: 1) creates QoS lanes with admission hints (fast/normal/batch), 2) performs token-aware admission and graceful degradation (partial response, compressed tokens, model-variant fallback order), and 3) exposes operator controls and SLO-driven automatic mode switching during failover. The system should bias towards preserving tail latency for high-SLO tenants while maintaining fleet stability and predictable cost.

Scope: Prototype and production rollout of admission controller and QoS lanes on the serving control plane, changes to request routing metadata (admit-hint, tokenEstimate, fidelityBudget), operator console controls and dashboards, and playbook updates for multi-region failover. Does NOT include client SDK changes beyond adding optional admit hints (separate client SDK ticket).
acceptance_criteria: Admission controller supports three QoS lanes (fast, normal, batch) and respects tenant priority + admit-hint metadata.
Token-aware admission logic estimates token cost from prompt metadata and applies dynamic budgets per-tenant per-window.

Graceful degrade modes implemented: (A) partial prefix-only response with clear truncation marker, (B) compressed token response (basic token trimming + summarization fallback), (C) model-variant fallback chain (quantized small model -> distilled model -> cached-prefix response).
System triggers auto-switch to conservative shedding policy during region overload and multi-region failover within configured SLO thresholds (p99 latency and availability).
Operator console exposes a rollback and manual override toggle and shows per-tenant queue lengths, admitted/denied counts, and estimated cost savings in a 1h window.
End-to-end tests validating: end-user observability (logs/trace tags), correct metric emission (shed_count, admit_rate, avg_truncated_tokens), and a staged rollout plan with canary traffic.
design_decisions: Use request-side tokenEstimate header populated by front proxy based on prompt length heuristics instead of deep payload inspection to keep admission cheap.
Admission policy will combine tenant-credit buckets (long-term reserved) + short-term burst tokens (leaky bucket) so enterprise customers with reserved capacity are protected by default.

Graceful degrade precedence: try partial-response (trim trailing tokens) -> summarization/compression transform -> model-variant fallback -> hard reject. This preserves some utility for most requests.
Prefer conservative defaults for auto-shedding thresholds tied to SLO windows (increase sensitivity near p99 breach). Operators can opt into aggressive cost-saving mode.
Avoid client-visible changes except optional admit-hint to preserve SDK compatibility. Detailed behaviour documented for clients wanting predictable truncation semantics.
tradeoffs: Partial responses reduce customer-perceived correctness for some workloads (e.g., code generation) but preserve latency and availability for high-priority tenants.
Estimating token cost heuristically can mispredict in edge cases; we mitigate with conservative buffers and learning-based calibration later.
Adding QoS lanes increases scheduler complexity and cross-tenant fairness subtlety; we accept this for improved tail protection for high-SLO tenants.
Model-variant fallback reduces quality but avoids full rejection; requires maintaining smaller model variants operationally which increases infra surface area.
implementation_notes: Control plane: add AdmitController module with pluggable policy hooks (tenantPriority, tokenBudget, historicalAdmitRate).
Runtime: add QoS lane metadata to request context and fast path checks before costly kernel scheduling work to avoid wasted GPU cycles for denied requests.
KV/Cache: when truncation or fallback is applied, store 'response_reason' and 'degraded_variant' tags in trace and cached artifacts for later evals.
API: agree on optional 'X-Admit-Hint: fast|normal|batch' header and 'X-Token-Estimate' integer; front proxy will compute token estimate using tokenizer library v2.
Metrics: emit admit_decision{tenant,reason,qos}, truncated_token_count, fallback_model, and per-tenant budget_consumed gauges.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (Canary): deploy AdmitController in staging + 5% production traffic for internal test tenants. Validate metric emission and low false-deny rate. (2 days)
Phase 2 (Selective Opt-in): enable for select enterprise tenants who agreed to soft-degrade testing. Monitor p99, error budget burn, and customer feedback. (1 week)
Phase 3 (Autoswitch Beta): enable automatic SLO-driven auto-shedding in 2 regions with operator observability. Keep manual kill switch. (2 weeks)
Phase 4 (GA): full rollout with dashboard default visibility and documentation. Backfill SDK docs for admit-hint. (post-signoff)
Rollback: immediate global toggle to disable shedding module and fall back to existing priority token buckets. Runbook located in links.
monitoring_and_slos: Primary SLOs: availability >= 99.95% (regional), p99 latency < configured tenant SLO (default 2s for fast lane).
Trigger conditions: if regional p99 latency increases by >25% over baseline AND admit_rate drops < 80% for 5m -> trigger conservative auto-shedding mode.
Alerting: Pager duty if shed_count for any high-SLA tenant > 0.5% of requests in 15 min window or if admission controller error rate > 0.1%.
Dashboards: QoS lane traffic volumes, per-tenant admit/deny, truncated_token_histogram, fallback_model_ratio, region-overload heatmap.
test_plan: Unit tests for AdmitController logic (priority + token buckets + burst logic).
Integration tests simulating multi-region failover with synthetic load to validate auto-switch behavior and safe rollback.
Chaos tests: introduce transient shard oom and verify graceful degrade precedence behaves as expected.
E2E canary runbook with test tenants exercising edge cases: long prompts, long-running streaming responses, tool-calling flows.
open_questions: How aggressive should default tokenEstimate buffers be for different model families? (initial conservative buffer = 15%).
Should we add a learning component to re-calibrate tokenEstimates per-tenant after 24h? (proposal in design doc).
What user-facing header or response metadata do we standardize for truncated responses so clients can retry deterministically?
Operational cost: who owns the smaller model variants (runtime or model-onboarding team)? Need clear SLOs for those models.
